assumptions: The initial target is Polish private outpatient clinics rather than public providers.
The founder remains employed and can devote approximately 15-20 hours weekly within the stated five-hour daily limit.
Clinics, not patients or insurers, would pay both the platform fee and any verified performance fee.
GDPR-compliant processing and clinic-directed messaging are obtainable in principle, but no access right or contract is assumed.
The proposed 300-clinic scale and 5 million PLN founder-net-worth path are projections rather than validated outcomes.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A paid Polish clinic pilot should show specialty-level baseline no-shows, cancellation timing, incremental filled visits against a credible control, collected recovered revenue, acceptance of the proposed subscription and performance fee, implementation and support hours, fully loaded contribution margin, CAC and sales cycle, renewal intent, and signed lawful access to scheduling, messaging, and attendance data. Evidence that the lift persists beyond incumbent reminders, waiting lists, or prepayment would be especially important.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Linking cancellation, waitlist matching, attendance, and recovered-revenue attribution targets a real utilization loss and creates a measurable outcome around which pricing could be built. The insight is useful but not novel at the workflow level because an established Polish incumbent already combines reminders, payments, and waiting-list filling.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Unused appointment capacity is a recurring operational problem, and private clinics demonstrably attach monetary value to reserved slots and buy scheduling software. However, setting-specific evidence shows attendance improvement does not necessarily increase reimbursement, while Polish clinic willingness to pay 900-2,500 PLN plus a performance fee has not been validated.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Prepaid subscriptions plus outcome fees could provide recurring revenue, good cash conversion, and low messaging costs. The proposed margins, CAC, implementation effort, attribution rules, retention, and owner earnings remain assumptions; pricing also sits materially above public incumbent practitioner plans, and compliance, integration, sales, and support may dominate costs.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish private outpatient clinics are a coherent beachhead, especially specialties with expensive appointments, material no-shows, and refillable demand. The supplied evidence does not quantify the number of suitable clinics, specialty-level loss, cancellation lead times, or attainable revenue, so the economically serviceable segment remains uncertain.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: The proposed vendor-neutral attribution and outcome pricing offer a possible positioning angle, but the candidate lacks clinic access, integration rights, exclusive distribution, or an owned transaction rail. ZnanyLekarz already controls calendars, marketplace demand, statistics, reminders, payments, waiting lists, and integrations, giving it a strong ability to bundle or replicate the offer.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: If the product wins a clinic workflow and proves incremental revenue, it could expand across specialties, clinic groups, geographies, scheduling optimization, recall campaigns, deposits, and broader capacity management. Those adjacencies depend on first obtaining lawful data access and proving a repeatable beachhead.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Permissioned multi-clinic response data could eventually improve models and switching costs, but no proprietary dataset, protected method, exclusive contract, durable integration, or mechanism ownership exists in the supplied evidence. Incumbents start with richer workflow data and can copy the visible features.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Outcome-based charging and cross-system attribution could make purchasing easier if they establish clearly incremental recovered revenue. Today the advantage is unproven against bundled waiting lists, reminders, online prepayment, and cancellation policies, while added integration and attribution complexity may offset convenience.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Digital clinic scheduling, messaging infrastructure, and contractible processor arrangements make deployment technically plausible, and clinics already purchase appointment software. There is no supplied evidence of a new regulatory, technological, or behavioral shift that uniquely favors this entrant, and incumbent maturity cuts against a strong timing advantage.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Integrator, accounting-partner, and referral channels are plausible in principle, and a CSV pilot offers a low-complexity validation route. None of those channels or clinic relationships is secured; integrations are controlled by counterparties, sales cycles and CAC are unknown, and the founder has no protected clinic-access advantage.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's quantitative skills, AI leverage, available capital, and proposed contractor support fit a part-time pilot. Execution still requires clinic sales, reliable reconciliation, health-data governance, messaging permissions, security, integrations, and management of attribution disputes; the critical agreements and operational inputs are all unverified.

highest_value_structural_change: Narrow the beachhead to one high-value specialty and secure a durable clinic or clinic-group agreement that grants lawful workflow access and permits controlled measurement, then sell only demonstrably incremental fills that existing scheduling software and prepayment policies miss. This would turn an unsecured feature bundle into a validated revenue mechanism with a credible path to proprietary data and repeatable integration.
main_structural_strength: The offer ties a recurring clinic utilization problem to a measurable transaction outcome, allowing a relatively capital-light pilot and potentially aligned recurring plus performance pricing.
primary_score_limiter: The candidate does not control the scheduling workflow, patient channel, integration, or proprietary mechanism, while a strong incumbent already bundles most of the proposed functionality and can respond cheaply.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: ZnanyLekarz already sells reminders, online payments, waiting-list filling, statistics, and external integrations in Poland, directly undermining the claimed differentiation; additionally, the cited randomized trial improved attendance without a statistically significant reimbursement increase.
